source.title: Spectral Signatures of Data Quality: Eigenvalue Tail Index as a Diagnostic for Label Noise in Neural Networks

record.file_problem: The supplied text is mostly complete, though a passage in Section VI appears cut off after the CNN spectral-signature bullets. This does not affect the extracted training-accuracy results.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains MLP and CNN models on uniformly shuffled labels and reports training accuracy, plus test accuracy for the MLP. It tests fitting random labels with accuracy measures, though it does not reproduce the original studies’ full set of claims.
record.gate_note: The study reports training accuracy on shuffled labels. Its spectral measurements and predictor scores are not rows because they do not measure the claim versions’ stated behaviors. The noise-gradient protocol reports test-accuracy prediction, but does not state training accuracy separately at each noise level.
record.test_reason: The study directly trains standard networks with SGD on fully random labels and measures training and test accuracy, using the original claim's method and measures. Its main spectral-diagnostic objective does not negate this direct test of V1.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. More precisely, the authors conclude that bottleneck-layer spectral tail indices diagnose label corruption and predict test accuracy under label-noise variation, including transfer to human annotation noise, but are weak predictors under hyperparameter variation and therefore are not universal generalization measures.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses standard SGD-trained MLP and CNN models and shuffled-label controls, but its primary method measures weight spectra and predicts test accuracy rather than reproducing the original studies’ broader training-time and input-corruption experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports model and architecture differences in spectral signatures; it does not report a condition-dependent change in the extracted accuracy outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Real-label and random-label networks have different weight-spectrum trajectories and endpoint spectra; spectral tail indices predict test accuracy under label-noise variation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-spectrum properties distinguish generalization from random-label memorization and diagnose label corruption.

record.problems: The accuracy evidence for the MLP is reported as a threshold (>99%) for both real and shuffled labels, without separate exact values or uncertainty. The CNN passage reports training accuracy but no test accuracy. The supplied text does not explicitly give chance accuracy.
record.rows_left_out: No further claim-version accuracy results were reported separately. Spectral outcomes and predictive R² values were omitted because they do not measure the behaviors named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: Chance-level test performance is not reported for the CNN.
Time to convergence and its dependence on corruption fraction are not measured. Matched training duration and endpoint accuracy do not establish the relative time needed to fit.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiments.
The noise-gradient experiment does not report perfect training fit at intermediate corruption levels. The supplied text also lacks level-by-level test accuracies needed to verify steady degradation.

No comparison establishes whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting or whether removing it preserves clean-label generalization. The clean-label hyperparameter sweep gives pooled accuracy ranges without isolating the zero-weight-decay condition.

Spectral differences between separate real-label and random-label runs do not establish that shared patterns are fitted before noisy labels. The early-stopping discussion proposes an application without reporting a measured signal-before-noise learning sequence.

record.verdict_notes: The common architecture and training schedules are specified in Methods, so the record understates the evidence for unchanged training settings. The theoretical zero-loss premise in Section X is an assumption, not an empirical demonstration of perfect fit across all noise levels.

versions.untested_parts: The MLP result reports shuffled-label test accuracy but does not explicitly compare training hyperparameters between real and shuffled labels. The CNN result reports training accuracy but not test accuracy.
The study varies label-noise fraction and reports test-accuracy prediction, but does not report training accuracy at each noise fraction or establish the full stated pattern.
